rules.statement: An ML-DSA (AKP) JWK writes `priv` as the 32-byte seed only, never the expanded private key, and writes `pub` as the raw public key.
rules.why: RFC 9964 defines the seed as the `priv` representation, and the seed is the compact, portable form.
rules.check: Look at AKP/ML-DSA JWK export or import code that writes or reads `priv` from the expanded private key (for example ExportMLDsaPrivateKey) instead of the private seed.

rules.statement: Suppress a BCL `[Experimental]` diagnostic (such as SYSLIB5006) only with a `#pragma warning disable` around the individual call site, with a comment giving the reason or the decision record. Don't suppress it project-wide, and use the stable members wherever they exist.
rules.why: Narrow suppressions can be deleted with no other change once the BCL drops `[Experimental]`, and they keep experimental use visible and justified.
rules.check: Look for NoWarn entries in project files, file-wide or assembly-wide suppressions of experimental diagnostics, a pragma with no comment, or experimental members used where a stable equivalent exists (for example the raw-key and seed MLDsa members).

rules.statement: Register an algorithm that depends on platform support (such as ML-DSA, gated on `MLDsa.IsSupported`) in the algorithm data source only when the running platform supports it, so that discovery metadata and the JWKS never advertise an `alg` that can't be signed or verified.
rules.why: Advertising an algorithm the platform can't fulfill is an interoperability bug.
rules.check: Look for platform-dependent algorithms added to the default algorithm registration without an `IsSupported` (or equivalent) guard.

rules.statement: Always register a key-type descriptor whose primitive depends on the platform, and throw `PlatformNotSupportedException` only when it is used on a platform without support. Don't make the descriptor's registration conditional.
rules.why: The key type stays part of the seam everywhere. Only the use fails on platforms without support, and only the algorithms are gated.
rules.check: Look for key-type descriptor registration wrapped in a platform-support check, or descriptors that fail silently or throw a different exception type when the platform lacks support.

rules.statement: Store asymmetric key material at rest as PKCS#8 (private) or SubjectPublicKeyInfo (public) DER, the same for every key family, not as raw key bytes or a JWK.
rules.why: The OID makes the parameter set self-describing, the encoding matches every other asymmetric family, and X.509 interoperability stays open.
rules.check: Look for new asymmetric key types whose serialization for storage writes raw keys, seeds or a custom format instead of PKCS#8 or SPKI DER.

rules.statement: Keep a parameter-set catalog that the specification closes (such as the three FIPS 204 ML-DSA sets) internal, and have callers select a set by its `alg` name rather than by a public parameter-set type.
rules.why: Each set is a distinct `alg`, so a public catalog adds surface without adding any choice for callers.
rules.check: Look for public types or public members that expose the parameter-set catalog of a closed algorithm family.

rules.statement: In a test project, make tests of a platform-dependent cryptographic primitive return early (no-op) when the primitive's `IsSupported` is false, so they run on every CI operating system and don't fail there.
rules.why: ML-DSA needs OpenSSL 3.5 or later, or a recent Windows 11, and the tests must run on every CI OS.
rules.check: Look for ML-DSA (or similar platform-gated) tests that have no `IsSupported` guard, or that are excluded from some CI platforms instead of being guarded.

rules.statement: Put an algorithm built on a stable BCL cryptographic primitive in the core libraries and register it by default. Reserve opt-in packages for algorithms that need a clean-room implementation or a third-party dependency.
rules.why: An opt-in package exists only to isolate such code or dependencies. Without either, it just makes a host take an extra step.
rules.check: Look for new algorithms over stable BCL types placed in a separate opt-in package or needing an extra registration call, or for algorithms with a third-party or clean-room implementation added to the core libraries.
